Triggers.value: People who are related to the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
I can't stop bad things from happening to me
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Bao had always found a quiet strength in his role as a chaplain, a sense of purpose in offering solace to others. But for the past eight months, since the attack, that purpose had felt like a hollow echo. It happened on a Tuesday evening after he had left the hospital, walking toward the crowded subway station. Three young men had cornered him in a narrow alleyway connecting two bustling streets. He remembered the press of bodies, the rough fabric of a hoodie against his cheek, and the overwhelming smell of stale cigarette smoke. One held him down while the others took his wallet and the silver watch his late wife had given him. What stayed with him most, however, was the sound of their ragged, heavy breathing in his ear and the frozen, fragmented image of his own face reflected in the screen of his stolen phone as it fell to the pavement.

In the weeks that followed, these fragments began to intrude on his days. The memory wasn't a story he could recount but a series of disjointed, visceral snapshots. He would be in the middle of a prayer and suddenly see the cracked pavement inches from his face, or be sitting in his quiet apartment and be ambushed by the scent of old smoke, so real it made him gag. With these sensory intrusions came a hot, helpless rage that felt alien and shameful to him. This fury was almost always followed by a cascade of self-recrimination. He had come to believe the event happened because of something inherently weak in him. A better man, a stronger man, would have fought back or wouldn't have been so oblivious as to walk down that alley in the first place. This painful conviction that he was somehow constitutionally flawed meant the memory was never far away; his thoughts would circle back to his own perceived failures, which in turn would conjure the very images he was desperate to escape.

This cycle of self-blame began to poison his perception of the world. Because he was certain he was uniquely vulnerable, a person destined for such things, he began to see threats everywhere. The belief that he couldn't stop bad things from happening made him scan every face in a crowd, his body tensing whenever he saw young men who remotely resembled his attackers. The hospital, once a place of sanctuary and service, became a landscape of potential triggers. The crowded corridors felt suffocating, each person brushing past him a potential threat. This heightened sense of danger only made the intrusive memories more frequent. Walking through the emergency department one afternoon, the sound of a patient's labored breathing was enough to plunge him back into the alley; he was suddenly overwhelmed by the visual of a snarling face above him and the feeling of powerlessness, his heart pounding in his chest.

The torment of the memory itself reinforced his vigilance. The sheer vividness of the images-the glint of a streetlamp off a worn sneaker, the pattern of grime on the brick wall-made him determined to avoid anything that might bring them back. He started taking longer routes to avoid crowds and began to dread his shifts at the hospital. The more he re-lived the memory, the more it confirmed his most painful beliefs about himself. The rage he felt upon recall wasn't directed at his assailants, but at his own helplessness, which served as undeniable proof that he was the sort of person bad things just happen to. He was trapped in a feedback loop: his sense of being a flawed person made him hyper-aware of triggers, the triggers summoned the memory, and the memory provided fresh evidence of his essential weakness.

His world has shrunk to his apartment and the quietest parts of the hospital. He makes excuses to avoid visiting patients in the bustling oncology ward and has stopped attending interfaith services. The isolation he has felt since his wife's death two years ago has become a profound and terrifying loneliness. He finally sought help when he realized he could no longer pray without the intrusive image of his own terrified face appearing in his mind's eye, a symbol of the man he now believed he was. He is terrified that this version of himself-weak, angry, and afraid-is the only one left.
